name: MCP Database Servers
title: MCP Database Servers
answer: Model Context Protocol servers expose a database to an AI assistant as a set of tools, such as listing tables, describing a schema and running a query. This site's MCP directory tracks active servers, including many for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and cloud warehouses. Of the 2451 active MCP servers tracked here, 263 are for SQL databases and warehouses. That is the scope: a bridge between an assistant's tool-calling interface and a database's query engine.

sections.body: Model Context Protocol servers expose a database to an AI assistant as a set of tools, such as listing tables, describing a schema and running a query. This site's MCP directory tracks active servers, including many for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and cloud warehouses. Of the 2451 active MCP servers tracked here, 263 are for SQL databases and warehouses. That is the scope: a bridge between an assistant's tool-calling interface and a database's query engine.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: MCP database servers typically run as a local process or a small remote service, speaking JSON-RPC over standard input and output or over HTTP. They connect to the database using the same client libraries and drivers that any application would use, so a PostgreSQL server uses a PostgreSQL driver, a MySQL server uses a MySQL driver, and so on. The server process holds the connection credentials and the query logic, while the assistant only sees the tool definitions and the results. Some servers are packaged as single binaries or container images, and some run inside the same environment as the assistant.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The server declares a set of tools, each with a name, a description and a parameter schema, and the assistant chooses which tool to call based on the user's request. For a query tool, the server receives the call, validates the parameters, translates them into a SQL statement or executes a prepared statement, and returns the rows as structured data. Many servers separate read-only tools from write tools, and some require the assistant to request a schema description before it can run a query. The assistant never talks to the database directly, it only talks to the server.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are credential exposure, over-permissioned database accounts, SQL injection through poorly validated parameters, and unintended data leakage when an assistant summarizes query results. Provenance matters because a server's origin, version and maintainer determine how much you can trust its tool definitions and its handling of credentials. Many servers are open source and can be inspected, but others are closed or distributed as binaries, so the audit trail is thinner. Access control usually lives in the database itself, so the server's database user is often scoped to the minimum needed for its tools.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The number of SQL and warehouse MCP servers is growing alongside the general MCP ecosystem, and more of them are adding read-only defaults, query timeouts and row limits. Expect tighter integration with agent frameworks, better schema discovery, and more attention to audit logging and permission scoping. The line between a database MCP server and a general data access layer is blurring, as servers add support for multiple engines and for semantic layers. Standardization efforts around tool definitions and authentication are likely to shape the next round of servers.
